title: Nvidia Halts GeForce RTX 5090 Production, Shocking Gaming Industry Fans
body:
Nvidia has quietly halted production of its flagship GeForce RTX 5090 graphics card, including the “D” variants that were earmarked for the Chinese market, according to a leaked internal memo from an undisclosed manufacturing facility. The abrupt cessation, which surfaced on a popular hardware‑leak forum, suggests the company is reassessing its high‑end GPU roadmap amid a confluence of supply‑chain constraints, shifting consumer demand and mounting competition from rivals such as AMD and Intel.

The leaked notice, posted by a well‑known leaker who goes by the handle “TechScribe,” indicates that the production line for the RTX 5090 was officially shut down last week. The document, which appears to be an internal communication to Nvidia’s manufacturing partners, cites “strategic realignment” and “market performance metrics” as the primary reasons for the decision. While the memo does not disclose specific sales figures, analysts have long warned that the RTX 5090’s premium price tag—hovering around $2,500 at launch—has limited its appeal to a niche segment of enthusiasts and professional creators. Early adoption rates were reportedly sluggish, especially in regions where the cost of high‑end GPUs is amplified by tariffs and import duties.

The move comes at a pivotal moment for Nvidia, which has been navigating a turbulent semiconductor environment since the COVID‑19 pandemic. Global shortages of key components such as high‑bandwidth memory (HBM) and advanced packaging materials have forced the company to prioritize its most profitable product lines. By discontinuing the RTX 5090, Nvidia can reallocate fab capacity to the more mainstream RTX 4080 and RTX 4090 models, which continue to see robust demand across gaming, AI, and data‑center workloads. Moreover, the decision may reflect Nvidia’s anticipation of the next generation of graphics architectures, rumored to be under development and expected to debut later this year.

Industry observers also note the geopolitical dimension of the “D” variant’s cancellation. The RTX 5090 D was designed to comply with China’s strict export controls, offering a version of the card that omits certain AI‑accelerating features. The termination of this line could signal a shift in Nvidia’s strategy toward the Chinese market, where domestic competitors such as Huawei’s Ascend series and the emerging “Kunpeng” GPUs are gaining traction. With U.S. export restrictions tightening, Nvidia may be opting to focus on products that can be sold globally without the need for region‑specific modifications, thereby simplifying its supply chain and reducing compliance overhead.

From a competitive standpoint, the RTX 5090’s exit opens a window for AMD’s Radeon 7900 XTX and Intel’s upcoming Arc A770 to capture a larger slice of the ultra‑high‑end segment. Both rivals have been aggressively pricing their top‑tier cards to undercut Nvidia’s premium offerings, a tactic that could attract the small cohort of gamers and creators willing to invest in the most powerful hardware. However, Nvidia’s entrenched ecosystem—spanning DLSS, Reflex and a mature driver suite—still provides a substantial moat that may mitigate the impact of the RTX 5090’s disappearance.

Looking ahead, Nvidia’s decision underscores the company’s need to balance innovation with market realities. While the RTX 5090 represented a technical showcase, its limited commercial traction appears to have outweighed the benefits of continued production. The firm is likely to channel resources into refining its upcoming Ada‑generation GPUs and expanding AI‑centric features that have become a major growth driver. As the graphics card market continues to evolve, Nvidia’s ability to adapt its product strategy quickly will be a key determinant of whether it can maintain its leadership position in both consumer and enterprise segments.
